Fort Worth Star-Telegram
February 2, 1998

By Bailey Ephland, Kennedale High [School] Eric Capp, Arlington Heights High [School] and Kelly DeGarmo, Star-Telegram Staff Writer section titled "Class Acts", which is targeted toward school children. (Ed. note: I graduated from Arlington Heights in 1958, and I remember that I disliked the late Robert Mitchum because he had been arrested for using something called "marijuana." I didn’t find out what hemp was for another twenty years. So much for a Yale education!)

"I think hemp jewelry is great," said Crissy Walters, an Arlington Heights High senior. "They should make more things out of it. It’s one of the strongest materials, and can outgrow things like cotton. Many different things can be made out of it, and weeds and droughts don’t affect its growth."

Hemp, one of the oldest cultivated fibers in the world, is weaving its way back to popularity.

It is sprouting up in fashion accessories and clothing, including items by Ralph Lauren and Calvin Klein.

"I think hemp jewelry is great," said Crissy Walters, an Arlington Heights High senior. "They should make more things out of it. It’s one of the strongest materials, and can outgrow things like cotton. Many different things can be made out of it, and weeds and droughts don’t affect its growth."

Indeed, environmentalists regard hemp as an Earth-friendly renewable resource with more than 25,000 commercial uses. Unlike cotton and wool, it requires minimum pesticides and chemicals to grow and process.

Hemp comes from the cannabis plant. Cannabis was once the most widely grown plant in the world, dating back 10,000 years, Hemptech President John Roulac told the ‘Star-Telegram.’ The California company is an industrial hemp information network.

The first two drafts of the Declaration of Independence were written on hemp paper and the Republic of Texas flag was made from hemp fabric, Roulac said.

But hemp is illegal to grow in the United States because it comes from the cannabis plant, the same species of plant from which marijuana is made. Commercial hemp comes from a different variety of plant, however.

In 1937, the hemp fiber fell victim to anti-drug laws. The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration still considers hemp the same as marijuana, although many countries permit commercial hemp farming, including China, Romania, France, Canada, Hungary, Spain, England and Germany. The U.S. legally imports tens of millions of dollars worth of hemp goods annually.

Because of its economic and environmental benefits, there is a movement to legalize commercial hemp. Threatened shortages of natural resources, such as timber and oil, are fueling a push by lawmakers, professors, farmers, company officials and celebrities to legalize the plant.

Hemp advocate and actor Woody Harrelson is endorsing the $80 Headwater Hiker hemp boots made by Deep E Co. For preservation of the Headwaters Forest in Northern California. Deep E Co. makes shoes, boots, hats, jackets, socks and other products from hemp.

"The more hemp fiber we use in making textiles, paper and other products, the less we have to rely on our diminishing forests resources," Harrelson states in the Deep E Co. spring 1998 catalog.

Young consumers are supporting the hemp fashions, priced from about $7 for a necklace to $180 for a jacket.

"I think it’s cool that hemp jewelry has been around so long," said Laura Lujan, a Kennedale High sophomore. "My mother wore hemp when she was my age, and I think it will continue to be in style for a long time to come.

About John E. Dvorak: John was born in Fort Worth, Texas, but is an eight year resident of Allston/Brighton, MA, where he is the proprietor of the Boston Hemp Co-op and Managing Editor of Hemp Magazine. He is a member of the Hemp Industries Association, the International Hemp Association, and Mass/Cann NORML.
